definition: Allay means to soothe or ease fears or concerns.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word allay. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know allay should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The coach's calm walkthrough of the backup plan helped allay the team's fears when the bus broke down an hour before the final.
Easing a worry only takes the edge off it; allay goes further, settling the fear until it stops nagging.
Banish outdoes allay: an allayed fear is quieted but may stir again, while a banished fear has been driven out entirely.

To soothe is gentler and more personal, working through tone, touch, or balm — you soothe a crying child or a sunburn. To allay is to quiet a fear or suspicion itself, and it usually works through facts: the test results, the signed contracts, the plain numbers.

Assuage is the broad word for making any painful feeling less intense — grief, guilt, hunger, and thirst can all be assuaged. Allay is narrower: it takes fears, doubts, and suspicions as its object and quiets them before panic can take root, most often by producing reassuring facts.
to sharpen a feeling instead of quieting it
to feed a fear or anger as you would feed a fire

Allay's Old English pieces fused long ago, so no prefix or suffix survives to reuse. Its only living cousin is the ordinary verb lay, and the family resemblance shows in the meaning: to allay a fear is, literally, to lay it down.
Allay means to soothe or ease fears or concerns.
When rumors spread that the mill would close, the owner did not send a memo — she walked the floor with the order book open, showing every crew the contracts that ran two years out.
By the end of the shift she had allayed the workers' fears without making a single promise beyond the pages in her hand.

Allay is sharper than calm or comfort because it acts on the feeling itself: you comfort a person, but you allay the fear, suspicion, or worry inside them — usually with facts, and usually before panic can take root.
Reach for allay when fears, doubts, or suspicions are the object: you allay a worry, usually with information.
Its cluster-mate pacify aims at an angry person rather than the feeling — you pacify a shouting crowd but allay its concerns.
In everyday speech, ease or calm does the same job more plainly.

The first rumor reached Marisol's teller window on a Tuesday: Harbor Savings, people whispered, was about to fail.
By Thursday a line stretched down the block, and depositors who had banked there for thirty years were demanding their savings in cash.
The bank's president understood that speeches would not allay a fear like this one.
Frightened people do not want promises; they want proof.
So on Friday morning she posted the bank's full balance sheet in the lobby window, invited the state examiner to address the crowd, and kept the doors open two hours late.
By Monday the line was gone.
The numbers had done what no reassuring words could do, and the fear quieted before it could become a panic.
